colossal

/kuh-LAH-sul/ — stress on LAH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something colossal is so large in size or scale that it stands out as far bigger than normal.

A colossal balloon shaped like a dragon floated over the parade.

Example

The ancient Roman aqueduct stretched for 60 kilometers across mountains and valleys, its colossal stone arches soaring so high that construction required scaffolding 40 meters tall.

Coloss (from colossus: a giant statue, like the Colossus of Rhodes striding over the harbor) + -al (characteristic of) = characteristic of a colossus—giant-statue huge. The arches are so enormous they rival the scale of monumental ancient structures, worthy of comparison to the Colossus itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

massive: Massive means extremely large, heavy, and solid — a massive boulder or vault door has weight you can feel. Colossal cares only about scale: it says something is stunningly far beyond normal size, whatever it weighs. Massive claims mass; colossal claims magnitude.

tremendous: Tremendous measures force, amount, or degree — a tremendous effort, a tremendous roar. Colossal measures physical size alone: giant-statue huge, dwarfing everything nearby. Applause can grow tremendous without anything getting bigger, but nothing is colossal unless its sheer size is what stands out.

titanic: Titanic means gigantic with a note of mythic power — the strength of the Titans, forces out of legend. Colossal is about visual size, not power: it says a thing looks overwhelmingly big. A titanic struggle needs no size at all; a colossal statue needs nothing but size.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tiny: very small in size

minuscule: so small it is barely noticeable

Where it sits · how far beyond ordinary size — big → huge → enormous → colossal

big vs. colossal: Big just means above average size, while colossal means so gigantic it leaves people awestruck.

huge vs. colossal: Huge describes something very large, but colossal pushes further, to a scale that seems almost unreal.

enormous vs. colossal: Enormous means remarkably large, yet colossal tops even that, suggesting the size of a giant statue towering over a harbor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — coloss(us)

Root — coloss(us): a giant statue, like the Colossus of Rhodes (Greek kolossos) (Greek (via Latin))

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of; relating to (Latin (-alis))

Put it together

Put it together: A colossus is a giant statue — like the bronze Colossus of Rhodes said to stride over a harbor — and -al means 'characteristic of.' So colossal means 'characteristic of a colossus': giant-sized, extraordinary in scale.

Use the root in a new word: colossus

Use the root in a new word: colossus: Ancient sailors told stories of a bronze colossus standing guard over the harbor at Rhodes.

Word Building

Word Choice

enthusiastic

Reach for colossal when size is not merely large but impressively, strikingly so—something that stands out and dominates your awareness through sheer magnitude. Unlike massive (neutral) or enormous (straightforward), colossal conveys drama and visual impact. Use it when describing monuments, natural wonders, or structures where the scale itself is the point.
